claims.text: What the strip looks like Three or more consecutive PVCs at a rate over 100, with a wide QRS (> 0.12 sec).
claims.quote: ≥ 3 consecutive PVCs at rate > 100 Wide QRS (> 0.12 sec)

claims.text: Aspects (abnormal in red) Rate: three or more ventricular beats in a row at ≥ 120 (Merck's definition)
claims.quote: Ventricular tachycardia is ≥ 3 consecutive ventricular beats at a rate ≥ 120 beats/minute.

claims.text: Some experts use a cutoff of ≥ 100
claims.quote: Some experts use a cutoff rate of ≥ 100 beats/minute for ventricular tachycardia (VT).

claims.text: Rhythm and QRS (monomorphic VT): regular, broad complex tachycardia, with every QRS identical in each lead (except fusion and capture beats)
claims.quote: Regular, broad complex tachycardia Uniform QRS complexes within each lead — each QRS is identical (except for fusion/capture beats)

claims.text: Favors VT: very broad QRS (> 160 ms), no typical RBBB or LBBB shape, extreme (“northwest”) axis
claims.quote: Very broad complexes (>160ms) Absence of typical RBBB or LBBB morphology Extreme axis deviation (“northwest axis”)
claims.locator: Other ECG features suggestive of VT

claims.text: AV dissociation: P waves and QRS complexes at different rates
claims.quote: AV dissociation (P and QRS complexes at different rates)
claims.locator: Other ECG features suggestive of VT

claims.text: Capture and fusion beats: a normal-width QRS when the sinus node briefly captures the ventricles; a hybrid QRS when a sinus and a ventricular beat coincide
claims.quote: Capture beats — occur when the sinoatrial node transiently ‘captures’ the ventricles, in the midst of AV dissociation, to produce a QRS complex of normal duration Fusion beats — occur when a sinus and ventricular beat coincide to produce a hybrid complex of intermediate morphology
claims.locator: Other ECG features suggestive of VT

claims.text: Concordance: chest leads all positive (R) or all negative (QS), with no RS complexes
claims.quote: Positive or negative concordance throughout the chest leads, i.e. leads V1-6 show entirely positive (R) or entirely negative (QS) complexes, with no RS complexes seen
claims.locator: Other ECG features suggestive of VT

claims.text: Josephson's sign: notching near the bottom of the S wave; Brugada's sign: QRS onset to S-wave nadir > 100 ms
claims.quote: Josephson’s sign – Notching near the nadir of the S-wave Brugada’s sign – The distance from the onset of the QRS complex to the nadir of the S-wave is > 100ms
claims.locator: Other ECG features suggestive of VT

claims.text: Most specific for VT: RSR' with a taller left “rabbit ear” (in RBBB the right ear is taller)
claims.quote: RSR’ complexes with a taller “left rabbit ear”. This is the most specific finding in favour of VT. This is in contrast to RBBB, where the right rabbit ear is taller
claims.locator: Other ECG features suggestive of VT

claims.text: Duration: sustained = > 30 seconds or needing intervention for hemodynamic compromise; non-sustained = three or more ventricular complexes ending on their own in < 30 seconds
claims.quote: Sustained = Duration > 30 seconds, or requiring intervention due to haemodynamic compromise Non-sustained = Three or more consecutive ventricular complexes, terminating spontaneously in < 30 seconds

claims.text: Treat any wide-complex tachycardia as VT until proven otherwise
claims.quote: Treat any wide-complex tachycardia as VT until proven otherwise

claims.text: A well-tolerated wide-complex tachycardia is not proof of SVT — some patients tolerate VT surprisingly well
claims.quote: Because some patients tolerate ventricular tachycardia surprisingly well, it is a mistake to conclude that a well-tolerated wide QRS complex tachycardia must be of supraventricular origin.

claims.text: Causes (mechanism and diagnoses) Re-entry (most common): scar from prior ischemia or infarction blocks one of two pathways, and impulses re-enter the blocked region to form a circuit
claims.quote: 1. Reentry (commonest mechanism) Requires two distinct conduction pathways Under normal circumstances, impulses cancel each other out (0) Conduction block in one pathway develops due to myocardial scarring, usually as a result of prior ischaemia/infarction (1) Strong ventricular impulses from the normal/slowed pathway can re-enter the blocked region (2), creating a re-entry circuit (3)

claims.text: Triggered activity: early or late after-depolarizations (e.g., torsades, digitalis toxicity); abnormal automaticity: a region of ventricular cells fires abnormally fast
claims.quote: 2. Triggered Activity Occurs due to early or late after-depolarisations Examples include Torsades de Pointes and digitalis toxicity 3. Abnormal Automaticity Accelerated abnormal impulse generation by a region of ventricular cells

claims.text: Most patients have significant heart disease, especially prior MI or a cardiomyopathy; contributors: hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, acidemia, hypoxemia, medication effects
claims.quote: Most patients with VT have a significant heart disorder, particularly prior myocardial infarction or a cardiomyopathy. Electrolyte abnormalities (particularly hypokalemia or hypomagnesemia), acidemia, hypoxemia, and adverse medication effects contribute

claims.text: Monomorphic VT: ischemic heart disease, dilated cardiomyopathy, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, Chagas disease
claims.quote: Ischaemic Heart Disease Dilated cardiomyopathy Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy Chaga’s Disease

claims.text: Symptoms Short or slow runs may be asymptomatic; sustained VT is almost always symptomatic — palpitations, hemodynamic compromise, or sudden cardiac death
claims.quote: Ventricular tachycardia of short duration or slow rate may be asymptomatic. Sustained VT is almost always symptomatic, causing palpitations, symptoms of hemodynamic compromise, or sudden cardiac death.

claims.text: Can cause hypotension, collapse and acute heart failure, from the extreme rate and loss of the atrial kick
claims.quote: VT may impair cardiac output with consequent hypotension, collapse, and acute cardiac failure. This is due to extreme heart rates and loss of coordinated atrial contraction (“atrial kick”)

claims.text: Low output can reduce myocardial perfusion and degenerate into VF
claims.quote: Decreased cardiac output may result in decreased myocardial perfusion with degeneration into VF

claims.text: Treatment Pulseless VT: defibrillation, starting at biphasic 120–200 J (or monophasic 360 J)
claims.quote: Pulseless VT requires defibrillation beginning with biphasic 120 to 200 joules (or monophasic 360 joules).

claims.text: Stable sustained VT: synchronized cardioversion at ≥ 100 J under conscious sedation or brief general anesthesia
claims.quote: Stable sustained VT can be treated with synchronized direct current cardioversion with ≥100 joules using conscious sedation or transient general anesthesia.

claims.text: Or IV antiarrhythmics: lidocaine (fast but often ineffective), procainamide (may take up to 1 hour), amiodarone (often used, slow); if procainamide or amiodarone fails → cardioversion
claims.quote: Stable sustained VT can be treated with intravenous class I or class III antiarrhythmics (1) (see table ). Lidocaine acts quickly but is frequently ineffective. If lidocaine is ineffective, IV procainamide may be given, but it may take up to 1 hour to work. IV amiodarone is frequently used but does not usually work quickly. Failure of IV procainamide or IV amiodarone is an indication for cardioversion.

claims.text: Do not give SVT drugs (e.g., verapamil, diltiazem) in VT — they may cause hemodynamic collapse and death
claims.quote: Using medications appropriate for supraventricular tachycardia (eg, verapamil, diltiazem) in patients with VT may cause hemodynamic collapse and death (2).

claims.text: Nonsustained VT: no immediate treatment unless runs are frequent or long enough to cause symptoms
claims.quote: Nonsustained VT does not require immediate treatment unless the runs are frequent or long enough to cause symptoms.

claims.text: Long-term: an ICD after sustained VT without a transient or reversible cause; a beta blocker with significant structural heart disease; amiodarone if an ICD can't be used
claims.quote: In the absence of a transient or reversible cause, patients who have had an episode of sustained VT typically require an ICD (1). Most patients with sustained VT and a significant structural heart disorder should also receive a beta-blocker. If an ICD cannot be used, amiodarone may be the preferred antiarrhythmic for prevention of sudden death.

notes.issue: quote did not say the antiarrhythmics are for stable sustained VT
notes.resolution: quote extended to start at the preceding sentence (class I or III antiarrhythmics); re-checked pass
